name: CV flow
seoTitle: CV flow Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: CV flow: work out flow rate from the inlet pressure and the pressure drop. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the CV flow calculator the inlet pressure, the pressure drop and the valve flow coefficient and it returns flow rate. Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the CV flow calculator work?
sections.html:
The CV flow calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports flow rate in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the liquid (medium)); then you type in the inlet pressure, the pressure drop and the valve flow coefficient (Cᵥ).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the CV flow calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Flow rate=the square root of (pressure drop) × valve flow coefficient (Cᵥ) ÷ the square root of (liquid (medium))
Outlet pressure=inlet pressure − pressure drop
Specific gravity=liquid (medium)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
The form opens with a complete set of values: Liquid (medium) set to Water. Straight away the calculator returns Liquid (medium) = 1.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Liquid (medium) = 1 should be roughly the size you expected from Liquid (medium) set to Water.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in liters per minute, and convertible to any of the 39 units on that chip.
  • Shown in kilopascals, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Flow rate, opening in liters per minute
  • Pressure, opening in kilopascals
  • Pressure, opening in kilopascals
  • Pressure, opening in kilopascals

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The CV flow calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the inlet pressure, the pressure drop and the valve flow coefficient — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the CV flow calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns flow rate, derived from the inlet pressure, the pressure drop and the valve flow coefficient. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the CV flow calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the inlet pressure, the pressure drop and the valve flow coefficient, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter flow rate in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Flow rate opens in liters per minute and the chip beside it offers 39 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Specific gravity = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the CV flow calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
